# Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?

Shengyun Si Junjie Chu Ye Leng Yang Zhang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding
author Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security

###### Abstract

Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort,
from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing
specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have
given rise to increasingly capable _Auto Researchers_, which can
autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end
research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how
closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers
align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate
this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: _Given
comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and
outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI
research?_ To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher–Human
Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for
assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research
artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152
ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories
spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to
these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently
fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts
across multiple stages of the research process.

## Introduction

![Refer to caption](2611.12429v1/overview_final_new_new.png)

Figure 1: Overview of our work. We construct AutoHRS by decomposing
human research into three stage-wise tasks: idea generation, experiment
design, and paper synthesis. Generated outputs are evaluated against
human research using a checklist-based evaluator validated by expert
judgments.

Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly integrated into
scientific research since their emergence, supporting tasks ranging from
scientific discovery to scientific writing \[[24](#bib.bib6),
[16](#bib.bib17), [1](#bib.bib2), [7](#bib.bib3), [13](#bib.bib4),
[15](#bib.bib8), [18](#bib.bib7), [20](#bib.bib5), [12](#bib.bib9)\].
Despite these advances, human researchers remained in control of the
overall research process, while LLMs primarily served as assistants for
individual tasks. With the development of harness-based agents, however,
language models are increasingly being integrated into end-to-end
scientific workflows \[[27](#bib.bib18), [23](#bib.bib19),
[22](#bib.bib20)\]. We refer to such harness-based systems that
autonomously carry out multiple stages of the research process as _Auto
Researchers_. In these emerging systems, the traditional division of
labor is substantially altered: auto researchers take a leading role in
carrying out the research process, while human researchers increasingly
provide guidance, feedback, and oversight \[[17](#bib.bib1),
[28](#bib.bib25), [31](#bib.bib26)\]. This shift raises an important
question of how the research produced by these systems should be
evaluated. However, evaluating research independently generated by auto
researchers is challenging: its novelty, scientific value, and potential
for genuine breakthroughs are difficult to establish without extensive
validation. A more tractable starting point is to use established human
research as a reference for assessing how these systems formulate ideas,
design experiments, and synthesize findings into papers. We therefore
ask: _Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions
in AI?_

Existing evaluation frameworks for LLM-based scientific research systems
have largely focused on model-level capabilities, typically assessing
performance on individual research tasks rather than the behavior of
harness-based systems operating across the full research
process \[[4](#bib.bib10), [25](#bib.bib11), [30](#bib.bib21),
[26](#bib.bib22), [6](#bib.bib23), [5](#bib.bib24)\]. In this work,
rather than evaluating auto researchers solely by whether they can
complete predefined research tasks, we ask whether they can conduct
research in ways that reconstruct the decisions and processes of human
researchers. To operationalize this evaluation, we introduce
AutoResearcher–Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise
evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers
reconstruct human research artifacts¹¹ 1 Reconstructing research
artifacts does not mean reproducing the original study; we use
reconstruction as a proxy to observe whether auto researchers can mimic
human research decisions and outputs. across different stages of the
scientific process. As scientific research is an open-ended, nonlinear,
and multi-stage process, we decompose it into three tractable stages
that can be systematically evaluated: idea generation grounded in
reference papers and a research direction, experiment design conditioned
on a given research idea, and paper synthesis grounded in provided
research context and experimental findings \[[14](#bib.bib30),
[11](#bib.bib29)\].

To instantiate this evaluation framework, we construct an evaluation
corpus from ICLR 2026 oral papers. Each paper is decomposed into three
research trajectories corresponding to three stages considered in
AutoHRS: from reference papers to a research idea, from a research idea
to an experimental plan, and from experimental findings to the final
paper. These trajectories provide both the inputs to the auto
researchers and corresponding human research outputs used as references
for evaluation. Our framework employs a fine-grained checklist-based
evaluation pipeline, with stage-specific dimensions and weights tailored
to stages of the research process. We further validate the framework
against human judgments, showing strong alignment with human judgments.

Our evaluation shows that current auto researchers exhibit limited
ability to reconstruct human research across all three stages. Under
AutoHRS, on a normalized scale from 0 to 1, auto researchers achieve a
score of 0.29 for the best-scoring idea per paper in idea generation,
0.36 on experiment design, and 0.65 on paper synthesis. To better
understand these results, we analyze where and how auto researchers
diverge from human research, identifying recurring patterns in idea
composition and experiment planning. We further analyze factors that
affect reconstruction performance, including the granularity of the
input research direction and the research type. These results suggest
that, despite their growing ability to automate end-to-end scientific
workflows, current auto researchers still differ substantially from
human researchers in how they formulate ideas, design experiments, and
synthesize research into scientific papers.

## AutoHRS Evaluation Framework

We propose an evaluation framework for auto researchers that assesses
whether they can reconstruct the research decisions made by human
researchers. In this framework, we define three stage-wise evaluation
tasks corresponding to three key stages of the research process:
literature-grounded idea generation, idea-grounded experiment design,
and findings-grounded paper synthesis.

### Stage-Wise Evaluation Tasks

Literature-Grounded Idea Generation. In this task, each instance
consists of a set of reference papers,
$`\mathcal{R}=\{R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}\}`$, and a general research
direction $`D`$. Each reference paper $`R_{i}`$ is represented by five
components, $`R_{i}=\{t_{i},a_{i},p_{i},m_{i},o_{i}\}`$, corresponding
to its title, abstract, problem, method, and results, respectively.
Given the reference set $`\mathcal{R}`$ and research direction $`D`$,
the target output is a structured research idea, represented as
$`I=\{p,g,r,m\}`$, where $`p`$ denotes the research problem, $`g`$ the
research gap, $`r`$ the research motivation, and $`m`$ the proposed
method.

Idea-Grounded Experiment Design. In this stage, the auto researcher is
given the structured research idea $`I=\{p,g,r,m\}`$ defined above.
Given the input $`I`$, the auto researcher is tasked with producing a
detailed experiment plan, denoted as $`P`$, that designs experiments
around the proposed method to evaluate whether it addresses the
identified research problem and gap. The plan is expected to specify the
main experimental objectives, evaluation settings, datasets or
benchmarks, comparison methods, evaluation criteria, and additional
analyses needed to test the proposed idea.

Figure 2: Overview of evaluation corpus construction.

Findings-Grounded Paper Synthesis. The final stage of the research
process is to synthesize experimental results and findings into a
research paper. In this task, the auto researcher is provided with the
research idea $`I`$, the experiment plan $`P`$, and the resulting
experimental evidence and findings, denoted as $`F`$. Given these
inputs, the auto researcher is tasked with synthesizing them into a
coherent research paper, allowing us to assess whether it can organize,
interpret, and communicate research findings in a manner comparable to
human researchers.

The input for each stage is independently extracted from the
corresponding target paper rather than generated from the output of the
preceding stage. This design allows each stage to be evaluated
independently without propagating errors from earlier stages. Details on
how task inputs and corresponding human reference outputs are extracted
and constructed are provided in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "Stage-Wise Evaluation Task Construction ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

### Evaluation Corpus

We construct the evaluation corpus from ICLR 2026 oral papers, using
each paper as the source for both stage-specific task inputs and the
corresponding human reference outputs. To prevent auto researchers from
directly retrieving information about the ground-truth papers, we
further restrict the corpus according to the knowledge cutoff of the
underlying models. We also manually screen the remaining papers and
remove those that do not satisfy the requirements of our evaluation
tasks, such as papers without publicly available reference papers and
purely theoretical papers without any experiments. Following the
stage-wise task definitions in
Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "Stage-Wise Evaluation Tasks ‣ AutoHRS Evaluation Framework ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
we then derive the corresponding evaluation instances from each paper,
pairing the stage-specific input with the human research output used as
the reference for evaluation. All stage-specific inputs and reference
outputs are extracted using an LLM-based pipeline and reformulated into
structured representations aligned with the input and output formats of
the respective tasks. Each resulting instance is reviewed and validated
by human annotators to ensure the correctness and quality of the
extracted content. After filtering and human validation, the resulting
corpus contains 152 papers and 456 research trajectories.

### Checklist-based Evaluation

At each research stage, AutoHRS takes an auto-researcher-generated
artifact and the corresponding human reference output as input. It
evaluates the generated artifact using a human-verified checklist
derived from the reference and produces item-level judgments,
dimension-level scores, and an overall score measuring reconstruction
fidelity.

Checklist Evaluation Pipeline. We design a checklist-based evaluation
protocol that enables reliable and reproducible automated assessment.
For each stage, we first extract checklist questions from the reference
output using an LLM generator. Each checklist question follows a general
form, “Does the output $`\mathcal{O}`$ contain or reflect the element
$`\mathcal{E}`$?”, where
$`\mathcal{O}\in\{\text{idea},\text{experiment plan},\text{paper}\}`$
denotes the auto researcher output at the corresponding stage, and
$`\mathcal{E}`$ denotes an element identified in the reference output.
An LLM then serves as a judge to evaluate the outputs generated by the
auto researcher, assigning each checklist item one of three labels: Yes,
Partial, or No. During preliminary evaluation, we found that some
checklist questions generated by the LLM were overly generic or
insufficiently discriminative. To improve checklist quality, we
introduce a human verification step in which annotators review the
generated questions and remove or revise those that are ambiguous,
overly broad, or uninformative for reconstruction evaluation. The
resulting checklist is then used to assess how well the auto researcher
reconstructs the corresponding human research output at each stage.
Further details on checklist generation are provided in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "Checklist Generation ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

Stage-Specific Evaluation Dimensions. Each stage of scientific research
involves multiple interconnected decisions and outputs, making it
difficult to characterize reconstruction fidelity with a single holistic
criterion. To enable a more fine-grained evaluation, we decompose each
research stage into a set of stage-specific evaluation dimensions. Our
dimension design is informed by established conventions in scientific
reasoning and reporting, including the CARS framework for framing
research problems and gaps, principles of rigorous and reproducible
experimental design, and the IMRaD structure for scientific
reporting \[[21](#bib.bib31), [19](#bib.bib16)\]. Specifically, (1) Idea
Generation: we evaluate the generated artifact along the dimensions of
Problem, Research Gap, Motivation, and Method. (2) Experiment Design: we
consider Experimental Objective, Experimental Setup, Baselines and
Comparisons, Evaluation Protocol, and Ablation and Analysis. (3) Paper
Synthesis: we evaluate Research Framing, Content Selection and Emphasis,
Scientific Argumentation, Information Organization, and Interpretation
and Positioning. Detailed definitions and the corresponding examples for
each dimension are provided in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "Checklist Dimensions ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

| Evaluator                | Idea Generation | Experiment Design | Paper Synthesis |
| ------------------------ | --------------- | ----------------- | --------------- |
| GPT-6 Astra              | 0.60            | 0.57              | 0.64            |
| Claude Fable 5.1         | 0.62            | 0.59              | 0.60            |
| Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B        | 0.58            | 0.50              | 0.55            |
| Checklist Metrics (Ours) | 0.70            | 0.64              | 0.68            |

Table 1: Instance-level Spearman’s correlation ($`\rho`$) with human
judgments across the three stages. Higher values indicate stronger
alignment with human annotators.

Validation Against Human Judgments. To validate whether the
checklist-based scores align with human assessment, we randomly sample
20 examples from the evaluation corpus and ask human annotators to
independently assess how well each auto-researcher output reconstructs
the corresponding human reference. We further compare our
checklist-based metric with a single-LLM-as-a-judge baseline. As shown
in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Checklist-based Evaluation ‣ AutoHRS Evaluation Framework ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
AutoHRS achieves instance-level Spearman’s correlations of
$`\rho=0.70`$, $`0.64`$, and $`0.68`$ with human judgments for idea
generation, experiment design, and paper synthesis, respectively,
achieving higher observed correlations than the single-LLM judges on the
annotated subset. These results indicate that the structured checklist
provides a more reliable proxy for human evaluation. Annotator
biographies, annotation details, and their responsibilities in the human
evaluation process, together with details of the single-LLM-as-a-judge
baseline, are provided in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "Biography of Annotators ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"), [A.5](#A1.SS5 "Single-LLM-as-a-Judge Baseline ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
and [A.6](#A1.SS6 "Human Evaluation for Checklist Validation ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

## Experiments

In our experiments, we leverage AutoHRS to evaluate auto researchers
using our curated human research trajectories as references. We then
analyze where and how auto researchers diverge from human research,
characterizing recurring patterns across different stages of the
research process. Finally, we investigate factors that can make
auto-researcher outputs more similar to human research, including the
granularity of the input research direction and variation across
different research types.

### Setup

Auto Researchers. We conduct our main experiments with Claude Code,
using Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the underlying model. We select this model
because its knowledge cutoff predates the target papers in our
evaluation corpus, reducing the risk that the model can recover
ground-truth research content from prior knowledge rather than from the
provided inputs. To assess robustness across agent harnesses, we further
replicate a subset of the experiments with Gemini CLI and Codex; setup
details and additional results are provided in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "Auto-Researcher Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
and [B.2](#A2.SS2 "Robustness Across Agent Harnesses ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

Data. We conduct our experiments on the evaluation corpus introduced in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "Evaluation Corpus ‣ AutoHRS Evaluation Framework ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
constructed from ICLR 2026 oral papers. The corpus is filtered according
to the knowledge cutoff of the underlying models and manually screened
to ensure that each paper supports all three evaluation tasks. The final
corpus contains 152 papers, yielding 456 research trajectories across
idea generation, experiment design, and paper synthesis. Each trajectory
consists of the stage-specific input provided to the auto researcher and
the corresponding human reference output used for evaluation.

Metrics. We use a unified metric formulation to evaluate auto
researchers across the three research stages considered in AutoHRS. At
each stage, the generated research artifact is evaluated along multiple
dimensions, as described in
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "Checklist-based Evaluation ‣ AutoHRS Evaluation Framework ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").
For each evaluation dimension $`d`$, the checklist-based evaluator
assigns a score $`s_{d,i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}`$ to the $`i`$-th checklist
item, corresponding to No, Partial, and Yes, respectively. Since the
number of checklist items may vary across dimensions, we first compute a
dimension-level score by averaging over all checklist items within that
dimension:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       S_{d}=\frac{1}{N_{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{d}}s_{d,i}
       ```                                             |     | (1) |

where $`N_{d}`$ denotes the number of checklist items associated with
dimension $`d`$. To aggregate dimension-level scores into an overall
AutoHRS score, we assign stage-specific weights to the evaluation
dimensions. The weights are selected based on alignment with human
judgments, using the weighting scheme that yields the highest
correlation with human evaluation for each research stage. Further
details on the weight selection procedure and the resulting
stage-specific weights are provided in
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "Weight Selection ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").
For a given stage $`t`$, the overall AutoHRS score is computed as a
weighted average of the corresponding dimension-level scores:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S_{\mathrm{AutoHRS}}^{(t)}=\sum_{d=1}^{D_{t}}w_{d}^{(t)}S_{d}^{(t)},\qquad\sum_{d=1}^{D_{t}}w_{d}^{(t)}=1
``` |  | (2) |

where $`w_{d}^{(t)}`$ denotes the weight assigned to dimension $`d`$ at
stage $`t`$, and $`D_{t}`$ denotes the number of evaluation dimensions
defined for that stage. Finally, we report
$`S_{\mathrm{AutoHRS}}^{(t)}`$ separately for each research stage.
Higher AutoHRS scores indicate greater fidelity in reconstructing the
corresponding human research output and stronger alignment with the
human reference.

### Main Findings

Figure 3: Idea generation results. (A) Distributions of overall AutoHRS
scores for every generated idea and the best-scoring idea for each
paper. “      ” indicates the mean and “$`\circ`$ ” indicates the
median. (B) Proportions of checklist outcomes (Yes, Partial, and No)
within each evaluation dimension, shown separately for the best idea per

Figure 4: Experiment design results. (A) Distributions of AutoHRS scores
for each evaluation dimension and the overall score. (B) Proportions of

Idea Generation.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Main Findings ‣ Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
shows that auto researchers achieve limited alignment with human
references in literature-grounded idea generation. The mean overall
AutoHRS score is 0.29 for the best-scoring idea per paper and 0.15
across all generated ideas. Regarding the proportions of checklist
outcomes, the results show that, for the best idea per paper, 42% of
problem-related checklist items receive a Yes, whereas the corresponding
proportions are 16% for research gap identification and 12% for both
motivation and method. Across all generated ideas, 24% of
problem-related items receive a Yes, while this proportion is only 5%
for each of the remaining dimensions. In both groups, No outcomes
dominate the research gap, motivation, and method dimensions. These
results indicate that auto researchers are better at recovering the
broad research problem than reconstructing the more specific research
decisions underlying the human reference.

Experiment Design.
Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Main Findings ‣ Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
shows that auto researchers achieve a mean overall AutoHRS score of 0.36
in idea-grounded experiment design. Alignment is strongest in
Experimental Objective, with a mean score of 0.52 and 42% of checklist
items receiving a Yes. The remaining dimensions exhibit lower alignment:
mean scores are 0.31 for Experimental Setup, 0.36 for Baselines and
Comparisons, 0.33 for Evaluation Protocol, and 0.38 for Ablation and
Analysis, with corresponding Yes proportions of 22%, 29%, 26%, and 30%,
respectively. No outcomes account for more than half of the checklist
items in each of these four dimensions. Although the overall AutoHRS
score is higher than in idea generation, alignment with human references
remains poor in concrete experimental choices, including experimental
setup, baseline selection, evaluation protocols, and ablation studies.

Figure 5: Paper synthesis results. (A) Distributions of AutoHRS scores
for each evaluation dimension and the overall score. (B) Proportions of
checklist outcomes (Yes, Partial, and No) within each evaluation
dimension.

Paper Synthesis.
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Main Findings ‣ Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
shows that auto researchers achieve a mean overall AutoHRS score of 0.65
in findings-grounded paper synthesis. Alignment is strongest in Research
Framing and Scientific Argumentation, with mean scores of 0.72 and 0.70,
respectively, and 68% of checklist items receiving a Yes in both
dimensions. Mean scores are 0.63 for Content Selection and Emphasis and
0.64 for Interpretation and Positioning, with a Yes proportion of 59% in
each dimension. Information Organization exhibits the lowest alignment,
with a mean score of 0.58 and 57% of checklist items receiving a Yes.
These results suggest that auto researchers are more effective at
reconstructing human research in paper writing than in earlier stages
when provided with the research context and findings. However, auto
researchers still differ from human experts in how they organize papers
and emphasize key aspects of the research.

### Where and how auto researchers diverge from human research

Reference-Driven Idea Composition. During manual inspection of
auto-researcher-generated research trajectories, we observed several
recurring patterns that may contribute to their divergence from
human-generated ideas. Auto researchers frequently construct new ideas
by combining or integrating elements from multiple reference papers,
whereas such patterns appear less frequently in the corresponding human
ideas. To examine this observation, we randomly sample 20 research
trajectories and manually assess whether each idea is primarily formed
by combining identifiable elements from the provided reference papers.
Under this criterion, 17 of the 20 auto-researcher-generated ideas
exhibit a composition-based pattern, whereas the corresponding human
ideas do not. We then extend this analysis to all research trajectories
using GPT-6 Astra to assess the relationship between generated ideas and
their reference papers. The results show that 78.4% of
auto-researcher-generated ideas exhibit this pattern, suggesting a
strong tendency to synthesize existing reference elements rather than
depart from them in the same way as human researchers.

Conventional Biases in Experiment Planning. Recurring patterns are also
observed in auto-researcher-generated experiment plans. Rather than
tailoring experimental designs closely to the specific research
question, auto researchers often fall back on conventional experimental
choices. They tend to select commonly used models and standard
evaluation metrics, while introducing task-specific or customized
metrics much less frequently. Together, these patterns suggest that auto
researchers often rely on generic experimental templates, which may
contribute to their divergence from human-designed experiment plans.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### How to Make Auto-Researcher Outputs More Similar to Human Research

We further investigate factors that may affect the reconstruction
performance of auto researchers. We examine how the granularity of the
input research direction influences idea generation, and whether
reconstruction performance varies across different types of research
papers, including Empirical, Methodological, and Benchmark-oriented
work.

Impact of Research Direction Granularity. In our main experiments, the
input to the idea generation stage consists of reference papers together
with a research direction. By default, the research direction is
expressed as a broad phrase, such as “LLM Reasoning”, “Multimodal
Learning”, or “Agent Safety”. In preliminary experiments, we observed
that providing slightly more specific research directions can improve
idea-generation performance. Motivated by this observation, we
investigate how the granularity of the research direction affects
reconstruction performance. We define four levels of granularity by
progressively narrowing the topical scope while avoiding information
that directly reveals the target problem, research gap, motivation, or
method. The four levels correspond to a broad field, a research topic, a
focused research area, and a fine-grained research scope. Examples for
each granularity level are provided in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "Granularity Examples ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").
Each level introduces only a modest amount of additional information
over the previous one. As shown in
Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ How to Make Auto-Researcher Outputs More Similar to Human Research ‣ Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
AutoHRS scores consistently increase as the research direction becomes
more fine-grained.

Figure 6: Impact of research-direction granularity on idea-generation
performance. Overall AutoHRS score at different levels of
research-direction granularity (L0–L3).

Performance Across Research Types. To examine whether reconstruction
performance varies across research types, we manually identify papers in
the evaluation corpus that fall into three categories: Empirical
Analysis, Method/Algorithm, and Benchmark/Evaluation. For each category,
we select 20 papers that match the corresponding research type and
evaluate idea-generation performance within each subset. As shown in
Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ How to Make Auto-Researcher Outputs More Similar to Human Research ‣ Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
auto researchers achieve the highest AutoHRS score of 0.49 on Empirical
Analysis papers, followed by 0.32 on Method/Algorithm papers and 0.18 on
Benchmark/Evaluation papers. These results suggest that the ability of
auto researchers to reconstruct human research ideas varies
substantially across research types, with benchmark- and
evaluation-oriented work being particularly challenging.

Figure 7: Impact of research type on idea-generation performance.
Overall AutoHRS score across different research types: Empirical
Analysis, Method/Algorithm, and Benchmark/Evaluation.

## Related Work

### Automated Scientific Research

Recent advances in large language models and general-purpose agent
harnesses have substantially broadened the scope of automated scientific
research. Early LLM-based work largely focused on individual stages of
the research process, such as idea generation, experimentation, and
scientific writing \[[9](#bib.bib27), [1](#bib.bib2), [8](#bib.bib12),
[17](#bib.bib1), [10](#bib.bib28), [2](#bib.bib13), [3](#bib.bib14),
[29](#bib.bib15)\]. More recently, harness-based auto researchers have
begun to operate across the full research workflow, shifting the role of
humans increasingly toward high-level guidance and oversight.
ARIS \[[27](#bib.bib18)\] enables end-to-end autonomous research through
adversarial multi-agent collaboration, while
Sibyl-AutoResearch \[[23](#bib.bib19)\], a self-evolving research
harness, improves through trial-and-error experience. In this work, we
focus specifically on harness-based auto researchers that carry out
multiple stages of the scientific research process in an end-to-end
manner.

### Evaluation of Auto Researchers

Existing evaluations of automated scientific research largely focus
either on model-level capabilities or on task completion within
individual stages of the research process \[[4](#bib.bib10),
[30](#bib.bib21)\]. RE-Bench \[[25](#bib.bib11)\] compares
language-model agents with human experts on open-ended machine-learning
research engineering tasks. IdeaBench \[[7](#bib.bib3)\] evaluates LLMs
on research idea generation, focusing on the quality of generated ideas.
In contrast, the systematic evaluation of general-purpose harness-based
auto researchers has only recently begun to emerge. The work
by \[[6](#bib.bib23)\] focuses on diagnosing and tracing the causes of
failures in end-to-end AutoResearch trajectories. A concurrent work,
ARAC \[[5](#bib.bib24)\], evaluates auto-research systems against
generalized human research methodology, whereas we directly assess
whether they reconstruct the specific research decisions of individual
human research trajectories.

## Conclusion and Discussion

We introduced AutoHRS, a stage-wise framework for evaluating how
faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research across idea
generation, experiment design, and paper synthesis. AutoHRS further
provides a fine-grained checklist-based evaluation pipeline with
stage-specific dimensions, and we validate its alignment with human
judgments. Our results reveal substantial differences from human
research across all three stages, with larger gaps in earlier research
decisions. Further analysis shows recurring patterns in how auto
researchers diverge from human researchers, including reference-driven
idea composition and conventional experiment planning. We also find that
reconstruction performance can improve with more fine-grained research
directions and varies across research types. These findings suggest that
evaluating auto researchers requires looking beyond end-to-end task
completion to the research decisions and processes underlying their
outputs. Future auto-researcher systems should therefore aim not only to
automate scientific workflows, but also to make research decisions that
more closely resemble those of human researchers.

## Limitations

Our study has several limitations. First, AutoHRS is evaluated only on
research papers from the AI domain, and it remains unclear whether the
observed patterns generalize to other scientific disciplines with
different research practices and evaluation criteria. Second, running
end-to-end auto-researcher trajectories is computationally expensive. As
a result, our main evaluation is limited to 152 papers, corresponding to
456 stage-wise research trajectories. While this scale is sufficient to
reveal consistent patterns across our analyses, broader evaluations over
larger and more diverse corpora would provide a more comprehensive
assessment of auto-researcher behavior.

### Single-LLM-as-a-Judge Baseline

This section provides additional details on the single-LLM-as-a-judge
baseline used in our validation experiments. Unlike AutoHRS, which
decomposes evaluation into checklist questions and aggregates their
outcomes, the single-LLM judge directly compares the auto-researcher
output with the corresponding human reference using the same
stage-specific evaluation dimensions and assigns a single holistic
reconstruction score.
Figure [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Single-LLM-as-a-Judge Baseline ‣ Appendix A AutoHRS Construction ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
presents the evaluation prompt for the idea generation stage as an
example.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 16: Prompt for the single-LLM-as-a-judge baseline, illustrated
using the idea generation stage. The judge directly compares the
candidate and human reference across the stage-specific evaluation
dimensions and assigns a single holistic reconstruction score.

### Human Evaluation for Checklist Validation

To validate the checklist-based evaluation against human judgments, we
conduct a human evaluation on a randomly sampled subset of 20 examples
from the evaluation corpus. For each example, annotators are provided
with the output generated by the auto researcher together with the
corresponding human reference output. Annotators are asked to directly
assess the overall degree to which the auto-researcher output
reconstructs the human reference, using a 5-point Likert scale from 0 to
4, where 0 indicates no meaningful reconstruction and 4 indicates highly
faithful reconstruction.

Each example is independently evaluated by three human annotators. We
assess inter-annotator agreement using the average-measures intraclass
correlation coefficient, ICC(3,3), obtaining a value of 0.72, which
indicates moderate agreement among annotators. We then average the three
annotation scores for each example and use the resulting mean as the
human judgment for correlation analysis with the checklist-based
evaluation.

## Appendix B Experiments

### Auto-Researcher Configuration

#### Research Skills and Execution Environment

We configure the research skills for the three evaluation stages by
adapting the instructions from \[[27](#bib.bib18)\]. The skills specify
the stage-specific inputs, task objectives, and expected output formats.
Each stage is executed independently using inputs extracted from the
corresponding human reference paper. We disable internet access,
including web search and external retrieval, to prevent access to the
target papers through online sources. The target papers and human
reference outputs are excluded from the agent-accessible workspace; only
the designated stage inputs are provided.

#### Idea Generation and Selection

We do not prescribe a fixed number of ideas per paper, allowing the auto
researcher to determine how many candidate ideas to produce during each
run. Consequently, the number of generated ideas varies across papers.
We evaluate every generated idea using the reference-derived checklist
and report results both across all generated ideas and for the
highest-scoring idea per paper. The best idea is selected post hoc
according to its overall AutoHRS score, rather than through a selection
rule specified in the research skill. The checklist and its scores are
used only for evaluation and are not provided to the auto researcher
during generation.

### Robustness Across Agent Harnesses

| Harness     | Underlying Model  |
|-------------|-------------------|
| Claude Code | Claude-Sonnet-4.5 |
| Gemini CLI  | Gemini-3.5-Flash  |
| Codex       | GPT-5.2           |

Table 3: Agent harnesses and their underlying language models.

To assess whether our findings hold across different agent harnesses, we
replicate a subset of our experiments using Gemini CLI and Codex. To
mitigate potential data contamination, we select underlying models whose
documented knowledge cutoffs predate the earliest public release of the
corresponding reference papers.
Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Robustness Across Agent Harnesses ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?")
lists the harnesses and their underlying models. As shown in
Figure [17](#A2.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Robustness Across Agent Harnesses ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?"),
the three harnesses achieve comparable average AutoHRS scores,
suggesting that our main findings are not specific to a particular
harness. Given the substantial cost of running large-scale research
trajectories, we therefore conduct the full evaluation using a single
primary harness and use the remaining harnesses for robustness checks.

Figure 17: AutoHRS performance across different agent harnesses. Average
AutoHRS scores of different harness-based auto researchers across the
three research stages: idea generation, experiment design, and paper
synthesis.

### Weight Selection

We initially compute the overall AutoHRS score for each stage by
uniformly averaging its dimension-level scores. However, uniform
weighting shows relatively limited correlation with human judgments,
indicating that different dimensions contribute unequally to
reconstruction quality. We therefore select stage-specific weights
through a grid search over non-negative weight combinations that sum to
one, choosing the combination that maximizes Spearman’s correlation with
human judgments. The resulting weights for each stage are reported in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Weight Selection ‣ Appendix B Experiments ‣ Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?").

|                     |                                  |        |
|---------------------|----------------------------------|--------|
|  Stage              |  Dimension                       | Weight |
|  Idea Generation    |  Problem                         | 0.20   |
|                     |  Research Gap                    | 0.25   |
|                     |  Motivation                      | 0.25   |
|                     |  Method                          | 0.30   |
|  Experiment Design  |  Experimental Objective          | 0.10   |
|                     |  Experimental Setup              | 0.20   |
|                     |  Baselines and Comparisons       | 0.30   |
|                     |  Evaluation Protocol             | 0.25   |
|                     |  Ablation and Analysis           | 0.15   |
|  Paper Synthesis    |  Research Framing                | 0.10   |
|                     |  Content Selection and Emphasis  | 0.25   |
|                     |  Scientific Argumentation        | 0.30   |
|                     |  Information Organization        | 0.25   |
|                     |  Interpretation and Positioning  | 0.10   |

Table 4: Stage-specific weights used in AutoHRS. The weights for each
stage are selected to maximize Spearman’s correlation with human
judgments under the constraint that they are non-negative and sum to
one.
